title: Global employment is stable at the headline level while job quality, income security and convergence remain under strain
source_unit: International Labour Organization, Employment and Social Trends 2026
geography: Global labour markets, with comparisons across country income groups and attention to women, young people, informal workers and trade-linked employment

unemployment.unit: per cent projected global unemployment rate

stability_quality_gap.value: The ILO says stable headline employment should not be mistaken for a return to healthy labour-market conditions because job-quality progress has stalled and exposure to economic, demographic and technological risks is rising.

policy_reading.value: The central signal is fragile stability: aggregate employment can hold while security, quality and distribution deteriorate underneath.

observations.method: ILO flagship report using modelled labour-market estimates, cross-country indicators and analytical interpretation of productivity, demographic, economic and technological pressures.
observations.uncertainty: The 4.9 per cent figure is a projection, not an observed final outcome; headline unemployment does not measure job quality, underemployment, informality or household security directly.
observations.subgroup: Workers and jobseekers globally, with risks distributed differently by country income group, gender, age, employment form and exposure to technology or trade shocks.
observations.counterinterpretation: Stable unemployment may reflect genuine labour-market resilience and could precede broader improvement if productivity, wages and institutions strengthen; the report's warning is not proof of universal deterioration.

observations.period: 2026 projection and latest available global estimates; unmet labour demand and job quality

jobs_gap.unit: people in projected global jobs gap in 2026

working_poverty.unit: workers living in extreme working poverty

income_recovery.value: Real wages and labour income had not fully recovered from recent inflation shocks according to the report.

observations.method: ILO global labour-market estimates and report synthesis; the jobs gap is broader than unemployment because it captures people who want paid work but cannot access it.
observations.uncertainty: The figures combine projections and estimates with different reference periods and definitions; they should not be added together or interpreted as mutually exclusive people.
observations.subgroup: Informal workers, people excluded from paid work, workers in extreme poverty and households whose living standards remain exposed to inflation and weak income recovery.
observations.counterinterpretation: Informal work can provide livelihood access where formal employment is scarce, and aggregate estimates may conceal improving conditions in particular countries or sectors.

observations.period: 2026 projection; income-group divergence, productivity and structural transformation

low_income_employment_growth.unit: per cent projected employment growth in low-income countries in 2026

divergence.value: High- and upper-middle-income economies benefit from ageing and slower labour-force growth stabilizing unemployment, while low-income economies face rapid labour-force expansion but weaker productivity and lower-quality job creation.

structural_transformation.value: The report says movement into higher-productivity and more formal sectors has slowed markedly over the past two decades.

observations.method: ILO comparative analysis across country income groups, with projections for employment and interpretation of productivity and structural transformation.
observations.uncertainty: Income-group averages hide large within-group differences; projected employment growth does not establish whether jobs are accessible, productive, formal or adequately paid for particular populations.
observations.subgroup: Workers and new labour-market entrants in low-income countries, younger populations in expanding labour forces, and economies seeking a demographic dividend.
observations.counterinterpretation: Rapid employment growth can build capabilities and future convergence if accompanied by skills, infrastructure, industrial policy and social protection; low current productivity does not make convergence impossible.

observations.period: 2026 report; gender, youth, trade and domestic policy capacity

gender_participation.unit: per cent lower likelihood of labour-force participation for women than men

youth_disconnection.unit: young people not in employment, education or training

trade_linked_jobs.unit: jobs linked to foreign demand worldwide

domestic_action.value: The report argues that progress will increasingly depend on domestic choices around job creation, productivity, skills, social protection and labour-market institutions as external financing and global growth remain constrained.

observations.method: ILO report synthesis of global labour estimates, trade-linked employment and policy implications; gender and youth figures are global estimates, not respondent-level observations in this record.
observations.uncertainty: The figures do not identify the causal contribution of discrimination, care burdens, education, health, macroeconomic conditions or institutions; trade-linked jobs are not necessarily secure or high quality in every setting.
observations.subgroup: Women, young people, workers in trade-linked sectors, small and medium enterprises, workers exposed to AI and workers relying on domestic labour-market institutions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Domestic policy is important but cannot fully offset global trade, debt, technology, demographic or geopolitical constraints; stronger external coordination may still be necessary.

related_sources.claim: ILO data and visualization resources for comparing labour-market trends across countries and regions.
Official DOI for Employment and Social Trends 2026.

boundary: This record adds a global labour-market layer: the ILO separates stable unemployment from job quality, informality, working poverty, income recovery, unequal productivity and access to work. It uses ILO modelled estimates and comparative synthesis, not respondent-level microdata, a household panel, transaction data or a causal evaluation of policy effects.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official ILO publication page was reviewed for the 2026 unemployment projection, global jobs gap, working poverty, informality, income-group divergence, productivity, gender, youth, trade-linked employment and domestic-policy messages.
